cover.headline: A global hotel platform whose costs have stopped outrunning its gross profit; at 29x Sep-28E EPS the price already assumes the Middle East heals
cover.lead: TBO Tek is a B2B travel wholesaler: ~159,000 agents in 100+ countries book hotels, air and ancillaries on TBO.com, and since Oct-2025 its Classic Vacations unit sells US luxury travel through ~10,000 advisors. Q1FY27 GTV rose 37% (organic +15% in constant currency) and EBITDA 84%, as organic SG&A grew only 4% in constant currency. We forecast EPS of ₹30.4 / ₹47.9 / ₹67.2 for FY27-29E, below the street in FY27-28E because we assume a slow Middle East recovery. The street values TBO on **P/E** (MOSL 35x and Anand Rathi 40x FY28E; Choice 35x FY28-29E). TBO listed in May-2024, so we start from its one-year-forward P/E median over the twelve months to 30-Sep-2026 (35.4x) and apply the same-window move of a widened travel + internet peer set (IRCTC, Thomas Cook, Info Edge, IndiaMART: −10%). **32x Sep-28E EPS of ₹57.5 = {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with HOLD.** With no sector move the value is ₹2,040; on the longer post-IPO window ₹2,360; the DCF gives ₹2,223. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: A real platform, now mostly international hotels
arguments.p: Hotels, ancillaries and Classic Vacations made ~90% of FY26 gross profit; agents outside India made 64% of Q1FY27 GTV and 89% of gross profit. Europe (+24% CC) and APAC (+41% CC) grew strongly enough to offset a flat Middle East: the diversification works.

arguments.h: Operating leverage has arrived, but it is the whole bull case
arguments.p: Organic EBITDA/GP rose from 23.5% (Q4FY26) to 27.5% (Q1FY27) as the KAM hiring cycle ended. We take group EBITDA/GP from 22.6% (FY26) to 25.1% / 29.9% / 33.6% (FY27-29E), so EBITDA grows ~37% a year on ~20% gross-profit growth. Scaled peers earn 45-60% of GP, so there is room, but management has said it may restart investment.

The rupee added ~11 points to Q1FY27 hotel GTV growth; Classic Vacations added most of the rest. Organic GTV grew +15% in constant currency and organic hotel GP/GTV fell as TBO cut prices to hold Middle East volume. Classic Vacations' own growth and synergies are "a few quarters away".

At ₹1,685 TBO trades at 55.5x FY27E, 35.2x FY28E and 29.3x Sep-28E EPS, against a 35.4x forward median over the past year; the four peers are 10% below their own medians. The street median target is ₹1,963; it is higher mainly because street FY27E EPS is 15-29% above ours. Pre-IPO funds still hold 22%.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): organic growth in the seasonal peak, hotel GP/GTV recovery, Classic Vacations in its weakest quarter.
Middle East travel: agent activity was back to Jan-2026 levels by Jun-2026, but management "has given up on predicting" the region.
Classic Vacations platform migration (targeted by end-CY2026) and the start of two-way cross-selling.
Acquisition-loan repayment from Q3FY27 (USD 70 mn over four years) and any further acquisition.
Block sales by pre-IPO funds (General Atlantic 14.4%, Augusta 5.1%, TBO Korea 2.9% in Jun-2026).

sections.title: A wholesaler of travel to travel agents: hotels make the money, air brings the traffic, Classic Vacations adds the US

blocks.p: TBO Tek runs TBO.com, a two-sided B2B platform. On one side are suppliers: 1 million+ hotels (directly contracted or through bed banks and channel managers), 750+ airlines (through GDSs, direct APIs and NDC), transfers, car rental, cruises and insurance. On the other are ~159,000 travel buyers in 100+ countries, mostly small retail travel agents, plus tour operators, OTAs, travel-management companies and loyalty programmes (enterprise buyers via API). An agent searches, books and pays on TBO in its own currency; TBO pays the supplier, carries the credit and handles the service. It earns a markup or commission: **revenue** is that margin for most bookings, and **gross profit** is revenue less service fees paid to partners. About 64% of FY26 GTV and ~87% of organic gross profit came from hotels and ancillaries; air tickets, sold mainly by Indian agents, are a low-margin traffic engine.

blocks.callout: **So what:** TBO is no longer an Indian air-ticket consolidator. Two-thirds of GTV and nearly 90% of gross profit now come from agents outside India (Q1FY27: 64% and 89%), mostly hotel business booked through its Dubai holding company. That diversification is why the business kept growing through the Middle East shock; it is also why the rupee now moves reported growth by up to ~11 points a quarter.

sections.title: Twenty years from a Delhi air consolidator to a global hotel platform: four acquisitions, three private-equity owners and a May-2024 IPO

blocks.p: TBO was founded in 2006 by Ankush Nijhawan and Gaurav Bhatnagar. It grew first as an air-ticket platform for Indian agents, went international from Dubai (2011), and bought its way into hotel supply and new markets: Island Hopper, Bookabed (2022), Jumbonline (Spain, 2023) and Classic Vacations (USA, Oct-2025, USD 125 mn). Naspers (2012), Affirma Capital (ex-Standard Chartered PE), General Atlantic (Oct-2023) and other funds were shareholders before the IPO. The IPO in May-2024 at ₹920 raised ₹400 cr of new money and let existing holders sell ₹1,151 cr. The stock peaked at ₹1,903 (weekly close) in Jun-2024, fell to ₹1,024 in Apr-2025, and traded between ₹1,068 and ₹1,711 in the twelve months to Sep-2026.

sections.title: Assisted travel is not dying: hotels are fragmented, agents need a wholesaler, and the rich are travelling more

blocks.p: Travel is sold to end travellers through three routes: suppliers' own sites (brand direct), consumer OTAs (Booking, Expedia, MakeMyTrip) and assisted travel through ~millions of retail travel agents, tour operators and advisors. B2B platforms such as TBO, Hotelbeds (HBX Group), WebBeds (Web Travel Group) and regional aggregators supply agents with inventory, payments and credit. TBO calls itself one of the top 4 B2B travel distribution platforms globally. Air is commoditised: ~300 airlines carry 80-85% of traffic, 40-50% of bookings flow through GDSs, and B2B take rates are ~1-3%. Hotels are fragmented: of 3-4 mn properties only 2-3% belong to major chains, so aggregation earns 8-10% take rates (Choice, 22-Sep-2026).

bullets: **Demand.** Global luxury leisure hospitality spend is forecast to grow from USD 239 bn (2023) to USD 391 bn (2028), HNI segments ~85% of the growth (McKinsey, May-2024, cited in TBO's Jun-2026 deck). India's outbound travel market USD 18.8 bn (FY24), expected ~11% CAGR to ~USD 55 bn by FY34 (Choice).

**The 2026 shock.** From Q4FY26 the Middle East conflict disrupted Gulf hub carriers (the East-West corridor), destination choice and sentiment; MEA was ~24% of TBO's FY26 hotel GTV and among its higher-margin markets. MEA GTV was flat in Q1FY27 (+1% in constant currency); India hotel GTV fell 2% as travellers rerouted east to cheaper destinations.

**Currency.** Most international GTV is in USD/EUR/AED; INR depreciation inflated Q1FY27 reported hotel GTV growth by ~11 points (49.8% reported vs 38.9% constant currency) and SG&A growth (12.3% reported vs 4% CC).
**Scale economics.** Management: scaled B2B peers (Hotelbeds, WebBeds) earn 45-60% EBITDA/GP vs TBO's ~26% (Q1FY27 call). TBO's organic adjusted EBITDA was 27.5% of gross profit in Q1FY27.

**Competition.** Global bed banks (Hotelbeds, WebBeds), OTAs' B2B arms (Expedia TAAP, Booking, MakeMyTrip, Yatra) and regional wholesalers all sell to the same agents, who use several platforms at once (Choice). TBO says it took share in Europe and APAC in Q1FY27 ("there isn't any organic growth in the market").

sections.title: Hotels: ~74% of gross profit, growing ~16% in constant currency, with margins dented by the Middle East

blocks.p: Organic hotels, ancillaries and other products (TBO without Classic Vacations) booked ₹21,745 cr of GTV in FY26 (+19.3% for hotels and ancillaries, AR) and earned ₹1,242 cr of gross profit, 5.7% of GTV. Growth comes from new source markets and cities, key-account managers (KAMs) hired in FY25-26 and more agents transacting each month; the margin comes from directly contracted supply (Platinum collection) and the mix of markets. In Q1FY27 organic hotel GTV grew +27% in rupees but only ~16% in constant currency, and GP/GTV fell to 5.3% from 5.6% in Q4FY26: the Middle East (a higher-margin market) shrank in the mix, and TBO chose to cut prices to keep volume "as long as incremental revenue remained contribution margin positive". Management expects GP/GTV to drift back towards its average.

sections.title: Classic Vacations: a quarter of gross profit at ~2.5% of GTV in EBITDA; the synergies are still ahead

blocks.p: Classic Vacations sells luxury hotels, packages and air to ~10,000 US travel advisors; revenue is booked when the traveller checks in, so Q1 (Apr-Jun) is its peak and Q2 its low. Since 1-Oct-2025 it has added GTV of ₹1,045 cr, ₹1,041 cr and ₹1,236 cr a quarter (net of TBO's own sales to it, ₹64 cr in Q1FY27) and gross profit of ₹131 cr, ₹139 cr and ₹167 cr. Its take rate is ~25% of GTV because it books gross revenue and pays about half of it on to advisors as commission; gross profit is ~13% of GTV. Adjusted EBITDA was ₹43.9 cr in Q1FY27 (3.4% of GTV); management calls ~2.5% for a full year "a fair assessment". The cost work (CRM, back office, more US sales staff) is mostly done; the revenue synergy (TBO hotels sold to Classic's advisors, and Classic's luxury supply sold to TBO's agents) needs the platform migration due by end-CY2026.

blocks.p: Airlines were ₹12,977 cr of organic GTV in FY26, 93% sold by Indian agents, but only ₹162 cr of gross profit (1.3% of GTV). The take rate has fallen from 2.6% (Q1FY26) to 2.2% (Q1FY27) as airlines cut commissions and push direct and NDC channels. Air still matters: it brings agents onto the platform daily and lets TBO cross-sell hotels, especially in India, where Q1FY27 air GTV grew 14.7% while India hotels fell 2%.

**Operating leverage.** TBO spent FY25-26 building its sales force (KAMs) in Europe, APAC, LATAM and the Middle East; organic SG&A growth peaked at ~29% a year and has slowed every quarter since, to 12.3% in Q1FY27 (4% in constant currency). Employee cost rose 17.4% (rupee and increments), hosting fell 13.7%, payment-gateway cost rose with retail GTV. Organic adjusted EBITDA rose 25% on 16% gross-profit growth: EBITDA/GP 23.5% in Q4FY26 to 27.5% in Q1FY27. We assume organic SG&A of ₹1,145 cr in FY27E (+11.5%, of which the rupee is ~6 points) and +10% a year after, against gross-profit growth of ~16-18%: group EBITDA/GP rises from 22.6% (FY26) to 25.1% / 29.9% / 33.6% in FY27-29E.

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict: a moderate moat.** TBO's advantage is scale: one platform, aggregated supply and credit across 100+ countries, which a small regional wholesaler cannot match and which lets each new market be added at low marginal cost. But it is not a monopoly: agents use several platforms, global bed banks and OTAs compete for the same bookings, and Q1FY27 showed TBO has to give up margin to hold volume when demand drops. The moat shows up in growth and share gains, not in pricing power.

sections.title: Revenue up ~8x since FY18 and profit up ~7x; the margin has fallen for three years as TBO invested and bought a lower-margin business

blocks.p: TBO's revenue was ₹343 cr in FY18 and ₹2,677 cr in FY26. Covid cut FY21 revenue by 75% (₹142 cr, a loss of ₹34 cr) because travel stopped. Since FY23, the first normal year, revenue has grown ~36% a year, but that number mixes three things: organic growth (FY26 organic revenue +23%, GTV +13%), the shift to hotels (which earn a higher take rate than air tickets) and, from Oct-2025, Classic Vacations, which books ~25% of its GTV as revenue. Net profit rose from ₹148 cr (FY23) to ₹244 cr (FY26), only 18% a year, because the EBITDA margin fell from 18.7% (FY24) to 14.1% (FY26): TBO hired sales staff in Europe, APAC and LATAM ahead of revenue, and Classic Vacations runs at a lower margin on its gross revenue. Depreciation and interest also rose with the acquisition.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean accounts, but profit is flattered by currency, amortisation is rising, and cash flow swings with the float

bullets: **Cash conversion is lumpy.** Cash from operations was ₹226 cr (FY24), ₹289 cr (FY25) and ₹-21 cr (FY26) against net profit of ₹201 / 230 / 244 cr. In FY26 receivables rose ₹726 cr: TBO stopped discounting Brazilian card instalments for a few months (an experiment reversed in mid-December, unwinding by Q2FY27), war-related collection delays and supplier incentives accrued through the year. The CFO calls it timing and expects historical (100%+) EBITDA-to-cash conversion again; Q1FY27 reversed part of it. Over FY22-26 operating cash flow (₹929 cr) was ~1.1x cumulative profit (₹857 cr).

**Other income is small and partly non-cash.** FY26 other income of ₹51.2 cr = interest ₹32.1 cr, liquid-fund income ₹2.5 cr, liabilities written back ₹15.5 cr and other items. We build FY27E as 3.5% on opening net treasury (₹836 cr) = ₹29 cr plus ₹20 cr of other items = ₹{{F.otherIncome.0|num}} cr, against ₹51.2 cr in FY26 and ₹51.6 cr annualising Q1FY27.

**One-offs:** acquisition costs of ₹14.5 cr (FY26), FX losses of ₹8.83 cr (FY26) and ₹5.5 cr (Q1FY27), exceptional gains of ₹2.4 cr (FY26). ESOP cost (₹21 cr in FY26) is a real cost; the company's "adjusted EBITDA" adds it back, our EBITDA does not.

**Amortisation of acquired intangibles** (Classic Vacations customer and brand assets) more than doubled quarterly depreciation (₹14 cr to ₹33 cr); goodwill of ₹555 cr is tested yearly, not amortised.

**Engine note:** our model scales working capital with revenue (−34% of FY26 revenue), so forecast operating cash flow (₹{{F.cfo.0|num}} cr in FY27E) is higher than profit and the cash pile grows fast. Real working capital moves with GTV, supplier terms and the season; treat forecast cash and the DCF as generous by ~₹300 cr a year.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** The audit (S.R. Batliboi, EY network) is unmodified and the disclosure is unusually rich (constant-currency, regional and organic splits). We flag AMBER for three things: profit is translated from many currencies at a time of sharp rupee moves; working capital is large relative to profit and swings by several hundred crore; and an open FEMA show-cause notice (₹49 cr of transactions; penalty of up to three times) is not provided for.

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 TBO held ₹1,592 cr of cash, bank deposits and liquid investments (₹1,984 cr at Jun-2026) against ₹756 cr of borrowings (the USD 70 mn acquisition loan, a EUR 6 mn working-capital line at Jumbonline and lease liabilities). Net cash was ~₹836 cr, ~₹77 a share, ~5% of the market value. The balance sheet is dominated by working capital on GTV: trade receivables from agents ₹5,314 cr (~53 days of FY26 GTV; Screener shows 724 "debtor days" because it divides by net revenue) and trade payables to hotels and airlines ₹5,422 cr. Working capital swings with the season and supplier terms: it absorbed ~₹420 cr in FY26 (cash from operations −₹21 cr) and released cash in Q1FY27. Goodwill was ₹555 cr (Classic Vacations ₹449 cr), so book value is ~35% intangible.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a well-run global platform at 29.3x Sep-28E EPS; HOLD, with the Middle East as the swing factor

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** one of the four largest B2B travel distributors in the world, founder-run, with ~₹37,000 cr of GTV, two-thirds of it international hotels, a new US luxury business (Classic Vacations) and a cost base that has just started to grow more slowly than gross profit (organic EBITDA/GP 27.5% in Q1FY27). Net cash ~₹836 cr; no dividend.

**What you are paying:** 55.5x our FY27E and 29.3x Sep-28E EPS. Over the past twelve months the market paid a median 35.4x one-year-forward for TBO; peers trade 10% below their own medians. On the street's method and the house multiple the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): HOLD. With no sector move it would be ~₹2,040; on the longer post-IPO window ~₹2,360; the DCF says ~₹2,223. The street (median ₹1,963) is more bullish because its FY27E EPS is 15-29% and its FY28E EPS ~9% above ours.
